title: Habits grow by use
hookLine: walk to become a walker, read to become a reader (Discourses 2.18)
carry: one ordinary step at a time

lines: A WEEK IN BED WITH THE FLU.
cards: After a week in bed with the flu, you get up and try to walk to the mailbox. Your legs feel like someone else's. A week ago you didn't think about walking at all; now it takes effort.

Nothing was injured. You just didn't use them, and they quietly got weaker. Epictetus used almost exactly that example, a person getting out of bed after ten days, to explain how everything in us grows or shrinks.

teach.b: This is Discourses book two, chapter eighteen. Every habit and every ability, Epictetus says, is kept up and made stronger by the actions that match it. Walking by walking.
Running by running. Want to be a good reader? Read.
A writer? Write. Stop reading for thirty days and do something else instead, and you'll see what happens.

teach.h: TEN DAYS IN BED, WEAK LEGS.
teach.b: Lie in bed for ten days, then try a long walk, and you'll see how weak your legs have become. So here's his rule, as plain as anything in the Discourses. If you want to be able to do something, make a habit of doing it.
If you don't want to do something, don't do it, and get used to doing something else in its place. Notice that second half. He doesn't just say stop.
He says replace. A habit leaves a space, and something will fill it. Then he turns from the body to the mind, which for him is the whole point.
Patience, honesty, gentleness, courage work the same way.
Each kind act makes the next one easier. Each honest answer makes honesty more natural.
And the other direction too: every time you give in to a bad reaction, you haven't just had one bad moment; you've strengthened the habit. Nobody becomes patient by reading about patience.
You become patient the way you become a walker: one ordinary step at a time.

how: Stoic practitioners often pick one small virtue to practice repeatedly, on the principle that each act strengthens the habit, and replace an unwanted habit with a chosen one.

o: a talent you're born with and can never change
a settled habit, grown by doing the matching acts
a curse that keeps a person stuck in bad ways

games.q: habits grow by use: tap the pairs.

s: Epictetus says just stop a bad habit and you're done
he says get used to doing something else in its place.
he uses the example of someone getting up after ten days in bed
they find their legs have grown weak.
for Epictetus, giving in once strengthens the bad habit
each bad reaction feeds the habit, not just the moment.

games.q: you want to stop a habit you don't like. what does Epictetus' rule in 2.18 say to do?
o: don't do it, and get used to doing something else in its place.
read about it until it goes away.
games.why: he says if you don't want to do something, don't do it, and accustom yourself to something else instead.

practice: Choose one small good act you'd like to grow: listening without interrupting, a kind word at the door, putting the phone away at dinner, pausing before you answer.
Picture doing it once, then again tomorrow, and the day after, and feel how the second time is a little easier than the first.

wordCard.voice: Hexis. Greek for a settled habit: Epictetus' rule, walk to become a walker, read to become a reader, and act patiently to become patient.

orig.note: Greek hexis: a settled state or habit, from the verb 'to have'; Epictetus says every hexis grows by matching acts.

carryVoice: Your line: one ordinary step at a time. Each repeat makes the next one lighter. That's four hundred twelve.
